clue.text: Disguised male questioned (6)

blocks.note: m = male, the abbreviation every form uses
to question someone is to ask them, and the past tense carries over

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here announces itself as an instruction, which is what makes a bare two-part charade hard to spot: 'male' looks like part of the scene rather than a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Masked means wearing a covering over the face, so the wearer's identity is hidden — the everyday adjective sense.

clue.text: Fail to attend precious flipping trip (7)

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the piece just named is written the other way round.

blocks.note: to miss a lecture is to fail to attend it
a precious one is a PET — a darling — and those three letters turn over

explanation.walkthrough: 'Precious' is working as a noun, the household darling, not as an adjective. Setters lean on that shift constantly, and it is what hides the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: A misstep is a stumble, which is what 'trip' names as a noun; the figurative blunder sense grows out of that literal one.

clue.text: Request for help involving Calvin Klein footwear (5)

definitions.note: 'Footwear' is a mass noun, covering a pair as readily as a single item, so it fairly defines a plural answer.

indicators.note: Anything that involves another thing has taken it inside, which is where those two initials end up.

blocks.note: SOS is the distress call, a request for help
the label's initials, as printed on the waistband

explanation.walkthrough: Calvin Klein is here for his monogram, not his clothing line, though the surface is banking on you picturing the underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Socks are footwear in the plain sense — the garment worn on the foot, inside the shoe rather than instead of it.

clue.text: Former ride-share company worker is vivacious (9)

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, and EX- is the prefix meaning former
Uber is the ride-hailing firm
worker = ANT, the insect that works

explanation.walkthrough: 'Worker' is almost always ANT in a cryptic, occasionally BEE. Bank that one — it comes up more often than any other creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Exuberant describes someone bubbling over with high spirits, which is the liveliness 'vivacious' names.

clue.text: Dish of unusual grain (7)

blocks.note: a rare event is an unusual one
a grain of truth is a bit of it — the tiny-amount sense, not the cereal

explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at cereal crops, and 'grain' is the piece doing the misleading: it has to be read as a small quantity instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarebit — Welsh rarebit — is melted cheese on toast, so 'dish' defines it by category rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Withdraw from English area after start of revolution (7)

indicators.note: It is positional: what was named before it goes behind the piece named next, so the single letter leads.
The start of a word is the letter it opens with, so only that one letter is taken.

blocks.note: the first letter of 'revolution'
E = English, as in the school subject
a tract is an area of land

explanation.walkthrough: The political surface is a decoy: 'revolution' is wanted for its opening letter alone, and a tract of land supplies everything else.
explanation.definitionFit: To retract a statement is to withdraw it — the same act of taking back something already said, in the same verb form.

clue.text: Traitor I love in proportion (5)

blocks.note: a rat is an informer or turncoat
taken as itself
love is a score of nothing in tennis, written as a nought

explanation.walkthrough: Tennis supplies the cryptic's favourite O: love is nil, and nil is drawn as a nought. It turns up in a clue most weeks.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio states one quantity relative to another, which is the mathematical sense of 'proportion' rather than the 'large amount' one.

clue.text: Pub ban before Scotsman gets savage (9)

indicators.note: Plainly positional: whatever has been named already is placed in front of what comes next.

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
to bar something is to ban it
Ian is the Scottish form of John and the crossword's standard Scotsman

explanation.walkthrough: Two identical pieces out of two unrelated words, one a place and one a prohibition — and a Scotsman in a grid is nearly always IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbarian is an uncivilised person, so 'savage' names the same figure as a noun rather than describing ferocity.

clue.text: Former X contributor without sway (6)

indicators.note: Split it as 'W out' — the word names a letter to be dropped instead of meaning 'lacking'.

blocks.note: 'W out' is the letter that has to go
X used to be Twitter, so someone posting there was a TWEETER — now minus that W

explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is one of the great cryptic double-crosses. The rebranding is doing the other half of the work: X only became X in 2023.
explanation.definitionFit: To teeter is to rock unsteadily on the spot, and 'sway' is that same wobbling motion as a verb.

clue.text: Protect upstanding US agent on border (6)

indicators.note: Something upstanding is stood on its end, and in a down entry a piece stood up reads from the bottom.

blocks.note: a FED is an American federal agent, here stood on his head
the end of a field is its border or edge

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints an honourable officer on patrol; 'upstanding' is really a compass direction in disguise. FED is the standard American agent.
explanation.definitionFit: To defend is to protect, a plain synonym — though 'defend' leans towards warding off an attack while 'protect' is the wider word.

clue.text: Uncle cuts up plant (9)

indicators.note: Read as mixed up rather than as a direction — in an across entry there is no upwards to point at.

blocks.note: the nine letters of UNCLE CUTS rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to picture an uncle pruning, so the fodder reads as a sentence rather than as raw material. The definition is the bare last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A succulent is a fleshy, water-storing plant such as an aloe, so 'plant' defines it by the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Short tenor getting refreshed on and off (5)

indicators.note: Doing a thing on and off is doing it intermittently, so the letters are taken intermittently too.

blocks.note: T = tenor, the voice part as marked on a score
every second letter of rEfReShEd

explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' is the definition, not an instruction to shorten anything — that is the trap. Count from the second letter, not the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse means saying something in very few words, so 'short' applies to the manner of speech rather than to height.

clue.text: Sample bit of pasta stealthily (5)

indicators.note: A bit of something is a part of it lifted out whole, so what is wanted is an unbroken run of the letters that follow, exactly as they are printed.

blocks.note: lying across the join: pasTA STEalthily

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sample' is a verb here, and it sits beside two food words that keep pulling it towards its noun sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste a dish is to sample it: both name the act of trying a small amount in order to judge the whole.

clue.text: Make speech after European scientist’s workplace gets involved (9)

indicators.note: Positional again: the speech-making named first is placed behind the two pieces that follow it.

blocks.note: E = European, the usual abbreviation
a laboratory, shortened as it always is
to orate is to make a speech

explanation.walkthrough: 'Involved' has to be read as the adjective meaning intricate, not as the verb it looks like at the end of that sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: An elaborate plan is a complicated one worked out in detail, which is the sense 'involved' carries as an adjective.

clue.text: Bill quietly left a club? (7)

blocks.note: p for piano, the musical direction to play quietly
L = left
taken as itself
clubs are one of the four suits, so a club is a card — the question mark owns up to the example

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a man slipping quietly out of a nightclub. Four pieces in a row with no indicator between them is what makes a charade this long hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A placard is a printed notice held up or posted, and 'bill' is the old word for exactly that — as in billboard and flyposting.

clue.text: PM behind expression of hesitation regarding accepting refusal (9)

indicators.note: To accept a thing is to take it in, so the refusal is admitted inside the letters already assembled.

blocks.note: aft is the rear end of a ship, so behind
ER is the noise made while stalling for time
a flat refusal is NO
a book on birds is a book regarding birds

explanation.walkthrough: In a clue stuffed with hesitation and refusal, 'PM' reads as a Prime Minister. It is the clock abbreviation, post meridiem — after midday.
explanation.definitionFit: PM stands for post meridiem, the stretch of the day that follows noon, so the abbreviation names that stretch exactly.

clue.text: Root of change I proposed initially (6)

indicators.note: Initially means at the outset, so only the opening letter of the word in front of it is used.

blocks.note: the tide turns — a turn is a change
taken as itself
the first letter of 'proposed'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Root of change' reads as an idiom about origins, which is the misdirection: 'root' is the definition all by itself, and 'of' merely joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnip is a root vegetable — the swollen root is the part eaten — so 'root' defines it by the bit of the plant that matters.

clue.text: Try rising during sincere broadcast for Grant (9)

indicators.note: In a down entry a piece that rises is read upwards from below, so it comes out turned round.
During means in the middle of, which puts one piece inside the other.
To broadcast seed is to scatter it by hand, and scattered letters land in a new order.

blocks.note: these seven letters are the material to be scattered
a try is a GO, rising in a down clue so it reads upwards

explanation.walkthrough: The capital G invites you to think of a man called Grant, and the definition hides at the end behind a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant a point is to admit it holds, the same acknowledgement a country makes when it formally accepts another's claim.

clue.text: Effigy of union’s leader embraced by nation (6)

indicators.note: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, so a single letter comes out of it.
To be embraced is to be held within someone's arms, so that letter sits inside the longer piece.

blocks.note: a state is a nation, and it opens up to take a letter in
the leading letter of 'union'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is trade-union politics, and 'union' is there only to lend its first letter. 'Effigy' is doing honest work as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An effigy is a sculpted likeness of a person, which is what the answer is — the word merely carries a whiff of bonfires and protest.

clue.text: Competitor in event ran tirelessly (7)

indicators.note: The smallest word in the clue is the instruction: what follows is holding the letters already, waiting to be spotted.

blocks.note: running straight across three words: evENT RAN Tirelessly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tirelessly' is lovely misdirection — it sounds like an instruction to remove something, and it is there to supply a single T.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrant is someone who has entered a race or contest, so 'competitor' names the same person, off the same list.

clue.text: Brief note concerning one Conservative snorting cocaine (7)

indicators.note: Someone snorting a drug is taking it inside, so that letter goes within the string built from the rest.

blocks.note: LA is the sixth note of the sol-fa scale
C is the standing abbreviation for cocaine — the piece that gets taken in
a talk on birds is a talk concerning birds
I is the Roman numeral for one
C = Conservative, as printed on a ballot paper

explanation.walkthrough: Two different Cs, one a political party and one a drug, sit two letters apart. The definition is the very first word, meaning short of speech rather than a legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic means saying a great deal in very few words, so 'brief' catches the manner of speaking rather than the length of a thing.

clue.text: Is a lie tricky to communicate? (6)

indicators.note: A tricky thing is slippery and awkward to handle, and letters like that will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: the six letters of IS A LIE rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries the joke: the clue asks whether a lie is hard to pass on, while quietly handing over its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To liaise is to act as go-between and keep two parties in touch, so 'communicate' names it in its cooperative sense.

clue.text: Be unfaithful to Charlie with passion and touching (5,2)

blocks.note: C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet
the heat of the moment — heat is passion
a hand on a shoulder is a hand touching it

explanation.walkthrough: Every piece is a straight synonym, so the difficulty is all in the surface, which sounds like an affair being confided rather than assembled.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheat on a partner is to be unfaithful to them; the phrasal verb keeps the same preposition the definition renders as 'to'.

clue.text: Small person parking next to quiet verge (6)

indicators.note: It asks only for adjacency, so the letter it moves could land either side and the crossing letters settle which.

blocks.note: SH is the noise you make to hush someone
the rim of a cup is its verge or edge
P = parking, as on the road sign

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is both words together, and the wordplay starts at 'parking' — a clean split that the roadside surface works hard to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a shrimp calls them undersized: a familiar mild insult borrowed from the tiny crustacean.

clue.text: That woman sorted out table with a hot drink (6,3)

indicators.note: Sorting something out means putting it into a different arrangement, which is what happens to those letters.

blocks.note: that woman = HER, untouched by the shuffling
the letters of TABLE and A rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled letters run straight across the gap between the two words, so the 6,3 in the clue tells you nothing about where the fodder ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbal tea is an infusion of leaves or flowers taken hot, so 'hot drink' defines it by category rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Disorganised leaders of army training session elicit apathy (2,3)

indicators.note: A leader is the letter a word opens with, and the plural asks for one from each word that follows.

blocks.note: the opening letters of all five words, in order

explanation.walkthrough: Five words in a row each giving one letter is a long acrostic, and the run has to begin immediately after the indicator — no gaps allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone all at sea is floundering and unable to get themselves in order, so 'disorganised' takes the idiom figuratively.

clue.text: Pleased with mouse finally finding space in forest (5)

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word before it, so only its closing letter is taken.

blocks.note: glad = pleased
the last letter of 'mouse'

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last three words together, and 'finding' is pure joinery — no letters hide in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A glade is a natural clearing among trees, so the definition describes it by the gap in the woodland rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Anticipate a pressure for auditor (5)

indicators.note: An auditor is a listener, so the piece is to be judged by ear and not by how it is spelt.

blocks.note: taken as itself
pressure is WEIGHT, and WEIGHT said aloud is what gets written down

explanation.walkthrough: Only the second piece is heard rather than spelt, so the A sits there untouched. A homophone need not swallow the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To await something is to anticipate its arrival: both verbs mean expecting it and holding off until it comes.

clue.text: Smooths out chains (5)

blocks.note: to iron a shirt is to press the creases out of it
restraints made of iron, worn around a prisoner's wrists or ankles

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, two definitions, no link word and no wordplay at all — the shortest clue in the grid and one of the harder ones to trust.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come off the metal: to iron is to press with a hot flat-iron, while a prisoner's irons are fetters.

clue.text: Mugger is idiot upset by six footer (9)

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
to ail someone is to trouble or upset them
an insect has six legs, and the crossword's insect of choice is the ant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Six footer' is not a tall man but a six-legged one. Count the legs whenever a height turns up in a clue — it nearly always means an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An assailant is whoever launches an attack, and a mugger is one kind of attacker, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: Quibbler holds new medallion (7)

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to keep it inside you, so the letter goes within the longer word rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a pedant quibbles over small points
N = new

explanation.walkthrough: PEDANT and the answer are a famous near-pair, one letter apart, which is why the quibbler turns up so often in clues of this shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendant is an ornament hung from a chain at the neck, which is what a medallion is once it is worn that way.

clue.text: Hammered bachelor put away (6)

blocks.note: B = bachelor, as in BA and BSc
to put away a big meal is to eat it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammered' pulls towards drunkenness, and the wordplay's 'put away' pulls the same way. The definition needs the other sense: thoroughly defeated.
explanation.definitionFit: A hammered team has been beaten heavily, so definition and answer share the past-participle sense of soundly defeated.
